claims.text: Work on the Gothic cathedral of Amiens began in 1220, after a disastrous fire; its main roof was not finished until about 1310.

An inscription on the south transept façade records that the foundation stone was laid in 1220
The main roof was not finished until c.1310.

claims.text: The high vault of Amiens Cathedral rises more than 42 metres (Columbia's Amiens project gives 43.3 m); Beauvais is a few metres higher.

evidence.excerpt: Amiens at 43.3 meters is a little lower than Beauvais at 46m.
Its vault rises to nearly 47 m, 4 m higher than Amiens.

claims.assumptions: Published heights differ: Columbia gives Amiens 43.3 m and Beauvais 46 m; the Beauvais association gives Beauvais nearly 47 m and 4 m more than Amiens. The film says only 'more than 42 metres' for Amiens, which all of these support.

The choir has the tallest vault of any Gothic choir: 46.7 m.
Its choir vaults rise above 48 metres
Amiens at 43.3 meters is a little lower than Beauvais at 46m.

claims.text: The eastern arm of a cathedral is commonly called the choir; the long body of the building is crossed by a cross-arm, the transept, and the piers where they meet are the crossing piers.

evidence.excerpt: The eastern arm of the cathedral is commonly called the choir
the long, boat-like body of the cathedral is intersected by a cross-arm or transept

claims.text: Medieval master builders used geometrical rules developed through centuries of trial and error, scaling up proven proportions for larger elements; they had no knowledge of material properties or allowable stresses, yet many of their buildings still stand.

evidence.excerpt: The master builders of the Middle Ages were able to use geometrical rules, developed through centuries of trial and error, to build structural elements by scaling up the same proportions for new larger elements [Huerta 2004]. In those days, there was no knowledge of material properties or allowable stresses.
Yet, many of these architectural marvels are still standing in a state of equilibrium.

claims.intended_visual: Geometry card: one proportion scaled up
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: Engineers analysing historic masonry assume it has no tensile strength; stone has little or no tensile capacity, so a masonry structure collapses if it cannot contain a line of thrust in compression.

evidence.excerpt: masonry has no tensile strength; it can resist infinite compression; and no sliding will occur within the masonry.
Stone has no or very little tensile capacity, so, the structure would collapse if it cannot contain a thrust line in compression.

claims.assumptions: These are the analysis assumptions of limit analysis (Heyman), stated as such: 'infinite compression' is not narrated.
claims.intended_visual: 2D diagram: an arch, squeeze (compression) vs pull (tension)
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: Masonry structures usually fail through instability rather than lack of material strength; stresses are typically only a fraction of the stone's crushing capacity, and unlike problems in elasticity, stability problems can be scaled.

evidence.excerpt: In most cases, masonry structures fail due to instability rather than a lack of material strength [Heyman 1995]. Stresses in masonry structures are typically only a fraction of the crushing capacity of the stone. Therefore, rigid block models with the same proportions as the structures are good models to understand their stability. Unlike problems in elasticity, stability problems can be scaled.

claims.intended_visual: Small model and large model with the same proportions
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: The line of thrust is the path of the compressive force through the stone; a masonry structure in pure compression is in equilibrium only if a line of thrust can be found that lies entirely within the masonry; if no such line can be found, it collapses.

evidence.excerpt: This is a theoretical line, which represents the path of the resultants of the compressive forces through the stone structure. For a pure compression structure to be in equilibrium with the applied loads there must be a line of thrust that lies entirely within the section.
if a line that fits within the arch’s profile for the given loading can no longer be found, then the arch will collapse.

claims.intended_visual: 2D diagram: a conceptual thrust line inside an arch (no magnitudes)
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

evidence.excerpt: written by Robert Hooke (1635-1703) in 1675
As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch, translation by Heyman [1995].

claims.intended_visual: 2D diagram: hanging chain flipped into an arch
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: A vault does not only press down: it also pushes outward, like a bow being bent; this outward push is called thrust.

evidence.excerpt: A vault, whatever its shape, does not simply press downward: it also pushes outward, like a bow being bent.
In structural mechanics, thrust is the horizontal component of the force exerted by a vault or an arch on its support.

claims.intended_visual: Romanesque section: outward push at the springing
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: Medieval builders knew about thrust: an Amiens document calls the thrust in the arcade arches 'boutture'.

evidence.excerpt: A contemporary document reveals that the builders were well aware of the existence of "thrust" in the arcade arches--it is termed boutture.

claims.assumptions: 'Contemporary' refers to the late-medieval Amiens context of the paragraph (the 1497 crisis); the film says only that builders knew about thrust.
claims.intended_visual: NOTE on the thrust arrows

claims.text: Romanesque builders vaulted their churches in heavy masonry; its considerable outward thrust forced them to thicken the supports and outer walls, stiffened by buttresses, so windows stayed small and interiors were dark.

evidence.excerpt: Since the heavy masonry of the vaulting creates considerable outward thrust it has been necessary to thicken the main supports (no longer columns but compound piers) and outer walls which are stiffened by shallow buttresses. Windows are small. The interior is now dark
In Romanesque architecture, this oblique thrust is spread along the entire length of the wall, which must therefore be thick and pierced with only small openings to remain stable.

claims.intended_visual: Romanesque section: thick wall, barrel vault, small windows
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: Gothic builders stopped fighting the thrust of vaults with wall thickness and learned to channel it, through the pointed arch, the ribbed vault and the flying buttress.

evidence.excerpt: master builders stopped fighting the thrust of vaults with sheer wall thickness. They learned to channel it instead. Three technical innovations made this revolution possible: the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress.

This revolution is made possible through the use of pointed arches and lightweight rib vaults, but above all by the creation of rigid peripheral supports ( culées) from which flying buttresses can be launched to support the high vaults.

claims.intended_visual: Three tools card
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no forces, stresses, loads or safety factors beyond quoted facts

claims.text: A pointed arch is formed by two arcs of a circle meeting at a point; it exerts less sideways thrust than a round arch, which allows it to be raised much higher.

evidence.excerpt: the pointed arch is formed by two arcs of a circle meeting at a point.

evidence.locator: Arc brisé et voûte sur croisée d’ogive
evidence.excerpt: Il a pour avantage d’exercer des poussées latérales réduites, ce qui permet de l’élever nettement plus haut.
The pointed arch. Appropriated from Islamic sources and applied to reduce outward thrust.

claims.text: The pointed arch was not born with Gothic: examples appear in Burgundian Romanesque architecture, at the rebuilding of the abbey of Cluny around 1088, and Columbia's Amiens project says it was appropriated from Islamic sources; at Saint-Denis it was used systematically with the other Gothic innovations.

evidence.excerpt: The pointed arch was not born with Gothic art: examples already appear in Burgundian Romanesque architecture, notably on the rebuilding site of the abbey of Cluny (Cluny III), around 1088. It was at the abbey of Saint-Denis, under Abbot Suger between 1130 and 1144, that it was used systematically and combined with the other Gothic innovations.
The pointed arch. Appropriated from Islamic sources

claims.intended_visual: Timeline note

claims.text: Unlike a round arch, a pointed arch can span bays of different widths while keeping the same height at its crown, a valuable asset for keeping complex vaults regular.

evidence.excerpt: unlike the round arch, the pointed arch allows bays of different widths to be spanned while keeping the same keystone height — a valuable asset for regularising complex vaults.

claims.assumptions: Geometric property also shown on the card: a semicircular arch's rise is half its span.

claims.text: Columbia's Amiens project says that, following Hooke's hanging-chain principle, the pointed arch is closer to a catenary than the round arch and so is more efficient; a round arch pushes outward at its base and, if its supports spread, sags and cracks.

evidence.excerpt: the line of force in an arch will follow the line of a catenary arch--like a hanging chain
Since the pointed arch comes closer to the round arch to a catenary curve it is more efficient.

the line of force in the masonry of a rounded arch: it will want to push outwards as "thrust" at the base of the arch. As the supports open outward the arch begins to sag, cracking on the inside surface at its crown and on the exterior surface at its haunch.

claims.assumptions: The first sentence is garbled on the page; it is read as 'closer than the round arch to a catenary curve'. The page calls Hooke an 18th-century physicist; Hooke wrote in 1675 (CLM_114), so the film takes the date from the MIT source.

claims.text: At the abbey church of Saint-Denis, Abbot Suger built a west front with rib vaults and pointed arches between 1130 and 1140, then a new choir between 1140 and 1144 in which the pointed arch is used throughout, the vaults are all ribbed and monumental stained-glass windows fill the walls.

evidence.excerpt: Entre 1130 et 1140, l’abbé Suger (1122-1151) choisit de greffer sur la nef carolingienne de son abbatiale un massif de façade* voûté d’ogives* et structuré par des arcs brisés*. Puis, entre 1140 et 1144, il érigea un chevet*

Ici, l’arc brisé est généralisé (fenêtres, arcs formerets* et doubleaux*), l’emploi de la voûte d’ogives est exclusif, les supports appareillés sont supplantés par des colonnes monolithes, les murs intermédiaires des chapelles sont élidés et, enfin, des vitraux monumentaux dématérialisent l’ensemble.

La voûte d’arêtes et l’arc en plein cintre y sont employés de manière quasi exclusive.

claims.text: Arches were usually drawn full size on the ground and divided into voussoirs; a wooden template was made for each voussoir, and the stones were laid on wooden centering, removed once the mortar had set (at Amiens after a couple of months or so).

evidence.locator: Des modèles en bois pour les tailleurs de pierre
evidence.excerpt: La forme des arcs est généralement tracée au sol à l’échelle 1, puis divisée en segments qui correspondent aux voussoirs , pierres qui vont constituer l’arc, surmonté par la "clé de voûte". Des gabarits en bois sont préparés aux dimensions de chaque voussoir : ils servent de modèle aux tailleurs de pierre. Les voussoirs sont ensuite disposés sur une armature de cintres en bois que l’on retire une fois le mortier pris.

All concave surfaces (arches, vaults) were formed over rigid wooden centering : the carefully-cut stones were laid up with a thin layer of mortar, left in place for a period (a couple of months or so) and then the formwork was removed.

claims.text: Why the 1284 vaults fell is still debated: explanations include monolithic colonnettes and settling mortar breaking flying buttresses, gusts of wind setting the buttress system resonating, and slow differential settlement of the foundations; the 2024 study finds no geotechnical cause and argues that raising the vaults by several metres, against proven proportions, made the upper structure too flexible.

evidence.excerpt: Il existe trois types d’interprétations pour expliquer l’effondrement partiel de voûtes du chœur en 1284, deux en partie haute de l’édifice, une en fondation.
Il s’agit pour la première de la rupture de colonnettes monolithes solidaires d’une maçonnerie appareillée dont les mortiers auraient progressivement tassé, provoquant la rupture d’arcs-boutants
La deuxième invoque la mise en résonnance du système culée/arc-boutant au même endroit
causée par un vent en rafale
La troisième suggère l’existence d’un tassement différentiel lent dans les fondations
un raidissement généralisé des parties hautes atteintes. Elles s’étaient avérées trop souples, non pas en soi, mais en raison de la décision

en cours de chantier de surélever de plusieurs mètres les voûtes de la cathédrale. Cette décision dû être prise au mépris des dimensions choisies pour les parties sous-jacentes, des proportions éprouvées
We here show that nothing appears to justify a geotechnical origin in the 1284 collapse.
Ainsi, nous ne souscrivons pas à l’hypothèse d’une origine géotechnique dans l’accident de 1284.
